name: Black rice extract

card.summary: An anthocyanin-rich antioxidant extract from pigmented rice; lab and animal work is plentiful, but human skin evidence was not found.
card.aka: Forbidden rice extract, purple rice extract, Oryza sativa extract
card.note: Most research is in cells, animals or food science; small human trials are registered on other outcomes.

quick.overview:
Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation from the bran of dark-coloured Oryza sativa rice, concentrated in anthocyanins. It is marketed in supplements and some skin-care products as an antioxidant botanical.

Published work includes cell, mouse and fruit-fly experiments and food-science studies. Human trials exist as registrations on metabolic, cognitive and immune outcomes; none testing skin appearance were found.
quick.mechanism: Anthocyanins are plant pigments with antioxidant activity. Laboratory studies report that black rice extract raised antioxidant enzyme activity (superoxide dismutase and catalase) in cells and mice and reduced inflammatory signalling in macrophage cells.
quick.risks: No safety signals are described in the sources, and rice-based foods are widely eaten. Extract-specific safety data from human trials were not found. Anthocyanin stability and bioavailability are active research topics.

lead: Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation obtained from the bran of dark-pigmented rice (Oryza sativa), whose colour comes mainly from anthocyanins, the same family of pigments found in blueberries and purple cabbage.[1][2] The grain is also called purple or forbidden rice; reference sources describe the "forbidden" label as a marketing term tied to claims of royal-only consumption.[1]

The extract is used and sold as an antioxidant botanical, and its appearance-related interest has two strands. The first is skin: anthocyanins are antioxidants, UV light damages skin collagen through oxidative and inflammatory signalling, and in cell experiments black rice extract lowered markers of that damage and raised type I procollagen, so formulators propose it as a photoaging-protection ingredient.[3][4][11] The second is body composition: a 12-week randomised trial in obese postmenopausal women reported lower DXA-measured body fat with the extract than with placebo.[12]

Beyond those, laboratory work reports antioxidant enzyme induction and reduced inflammatory signalling in cells, and animal studies report effects on liver fat, kidney injury and lifespan in fruit flies.[3][4][5][6][14][15] Small human trials have been registered on metabolism, cognition, immunity and stress; no published trial on skin appearance in people was found.

paras: Black rice is a group of Oryza sativa varieties, some of them glutinous, including Indonesian black rice, the Philippine heirloom balatinaw, pirurutong glutinous rice and Thai jasmine black rice. Local names include chak-hao in Manipur and kavuni arisi in Tamil Nadu, India.[1] The grain is deep black, turns deep purple when cooked, and has a mild nutty taste; it is eaten as porridge, in desserts, in Chinese black rice cake, and in bread and noodles.[1] Cooked grain is described as about 100 kcal per 100 g, with roughly 21 g carbohydrate, 4 g protein and 1.8 g fibre.[1]

The black trait arises from changes to the Kala4 gene, which drives anthocyanin production, and spread through natural crosses and deliberate breeding.[1] The anthocyanins concentrate in the bran hull, at higher levels by weight than in other coloured grains.[1] Marketing often calls the grain "forbidden rice" on the basis of claims that it was reserved for Chinese royalty; Wikipedia suggests its rarity, colour and low yield may have fuelled the association.[1] Chemistry papers have identified the individual anthocyanins in black rice, among them cyanidin-3-glucoside, and measured their degradation kinetics.[2]

A 2018 study in the International Journal of Molecular Medicine exposed HaCaT keratinocytes and human dermal fibroblasts to UV radiation. The extract reduced basal and UV-induced MMP-1 expression in keratinocytes, decreased MMP-1 and MMP-3 in UV-irradiated fibroblasts, and significantly increased type I procollagen expression, without changing cell viability.[18] It also lowered UV-induced reactive oxygen species in keratinocytes, reduced p38 and JNK activity and suppressed AP-1 activation; mass spectrometry identified antioxidant flavonoids including cyanidin-3-O-glucoside and taxifolin-7-O-glucoside. The authors suggested black rice extract as a possible active ingredient against skin photoaging.[18]

Matrix metalloproteinases break down collagen in the dermis, and UV exposure raises their production while lowering collagen synthesis, which is the pathway the study targeted.[18] A 2021 mouse study of a fermented blueberry and black rice food in a model of atopic dermatitis induced by particulate matter and a chemical irritant also falls in the skin field.[7]
This work was done in cultured cells and animals. Human skin studies of black rice extract applied topically or taken by mouth have not been published.

A 2006 study reported that black rice extract inhibited LDL oxidation more than white rice extract ex vivo and increased superoxide dismutase and catalase activities in cells and in mice.[3] A 2015 study found that the extract suppressed inflammatory responses in macrophage cells through NF-kB and AP-1 pathways.[4] Mice on a high-fat diet had less liver fat after extract supplementation,[5] and fruit flies fed the extract lived longer.[6] A 2021 study tested a fermented blueberry and black rice food in a mouse model of atopic dermatitis.[7] Work on gut metabolism and prebiotic activity of its anthocyanins has been done in vitro.[8]

Other laboratory and animal work includes an extract that affected Helicobacter pylori-induced apoptosis in cells, germinated Thai black rice extract in diabetic rats, an extract that protected rats against ethanol-induced kidney injury, and a food-science study of black rice extract improving oxidised muscle protein gels.[21][22][23][24] A systematic review of ten Asian studies of pigmented rice compounds and breast cancer found all were in vitro, with three also using animal comparisons.[20]

Applied research is largely food science: fortifying bread with an anthocyanin-rich extract, pH-sensitive packaging films containing purple and black rice extracts, and microencapsulation to protect anthocyanins during digestion.[9][10][11] Black rice extract is also a listed ingredient in cosmetic and supplement products as an antioxidant botanical; anthocyanins are pH-sensitive pigments that change colour, which is why formulations are studied for stability.[2]

The randomised trial closest to appearance is a 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled preliminary study in 105 obese postmenopausal women from Korea, 88 of whom completed it. DXA showed significantly lower trunk fat, total fat and body fat percentage in the extract group than in the placebo group (each P = 0.04), while body weight, BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio did not differ significantly; the authors described the study as preliminary.[19] No published human study of black rice extract on skin appearance was found.

Registered human trials on black rice or its anthocyanins include bioavailability in healthy adults (n=20), cognition and BDNF in healthy subjects (n=12), immune enhancement from rice bran extract (n=120), perceived stress (n=80), metabolic syndrome (n=101), lipid status with bilberry and black rice anthocyanins (n=55), cardiometabolic risk factors in Filipino adults with pigmented rice (n=60), cognitive and microvascular function in older adults (n=24) and a glucose and lipid comparison of white, brown and black rice in healthy Korean adults (n=15).[12][13][14][15][16][17][25][26][27] Published results for most of these are not yet available.

timeline.event: A study reports that black rice extract inhibits LDL oxidation and raises superoxide dismutase and catalase activity.[3]
Mouse and fruit-fly studies report effects on liver fat and lifespan.[5][6]
A cell study reports lower UV-induced MMP expression and higher procollagen with black rice extract.[18]
A 12-week RCT reports lower DXA body fat in postmenopausal women.[19]

chain: Anthocyanins act as antioxidants and dampen UV-triggered signalling in skin cells
Less collagen-degrading enzyme activity and more procollagen in cell models
Possible support for firmer, less photoaged skin (proposed, tested so far in cells)
angle.text: Black rice extract is promoted as an antioxidant for skin, with cell studies showing less UV-induced collagen-degrading enzyme expression. A separate 12-week trial in postmenopausal women reported lower DXA body fat.
